en: CBC blood test: what every line on the report means
angle: The single most ordered test in the region. Walk the reader line by line down an actual CBC report: WBC, RBC, HGB, HCT, MCV, MCH, PLT. Use a table of every abbreviation, and a range-scale for haemoglobin with separate male and female zones. Anaemia is very common across the region so link the low-haemoglobin path clearly.

en: CRP test: what a high inflammation marker actually means
angle: CRP is ordered constantly and misunderstood constantly. Distinguish standard CRP from hs-CRP for cardiac risk. Explain that a high CRP says inflammation exists but not where. Range-scale plus a table of typical causes by CRP band.

en: ESR blood test: why it is high and what happens next
angle: Often paired with CRP. Explain the Westergren method, why ESR lags behind CRP by days, and the classic regional causes including tuberculosis and brucellosis. Compare ESR and CRP in a table.

en: Ferritin test: reading your iron stores correctly
angle: Ferritin is the best single measure of iron stores but rises with any inflammation, which misleads people constantly. Range-scale, plus the crucial point that a normal ferritin with a high CRP can still hide iron deficiency. Iron deficiency is very common in regional women.

en: Urine analysis: what protein, blood and leukocytes mean
angle: Line by line through a urine dipstick and microscopy report. Protein, glucose, ketones, nitrites, leukocyte esterase, blood, casts, crystals. Table of each finding and what it suggests. Cover how to collect a clean midstream sample properly.

en: Uric acid test and gout: the numbers and the diet myths
angle: Gout is rising with regional diets. Range-scale for uric acid, honest treatment of which foods actually matter versus folklore, and the point that a normal level during an acute attack does not exclude gout.

en: Which blood tests need fasting, and for how long
angle: Extremely high intent, very practical. Table of common tests against fasting requirement. Cover whether water, coffee, smoking, and medicines are allowed, and the Ramadan angle where people are already fasting. Steps visual for preparing correctly.

en: How to choose a reliable laboratory in the Arab world
angle: A genuine differentiator for this site. Explain accreditation (ISO 15189, CAP), internal quality control, external quality assessment, why the same sample can give two different answers at two labs, and what to actually ask at reception. Written from the author's own field, which is laboratory connectivity.

en: ALT and AST: what raised liver enzymes mean
angle: Fatty liver is extremely common in the Gulf and Egypt. Range-scale for ALT, the AST/ALT ratio and what it hints at, hepatitis and medication causes. Distinguish from the wider liver panel.

en: Creatinine and eGFR: measuring kidney function
angle: Creatinine depends on muscle mass so eGFR matters more. Explain the CKD stages in a table, why dehydration in a hot climate raises creatinine transiently, and the painkiller link.

en: Vitamin D blood test: how to read your result
angle: Deficiency is paradoxically severe across the sunny Middle East. Range-scale in both ng/mL and nmol/L because labs in the region use both, which confuses people constantly. Cite regional prevalence studies.

en: Thyroid antibodies: anti-TPO, anti-Tg and what they predict
angle: Sits alongside the existing TSH guide. Autoimmune thyroid disease, what a positive antibody means when TSH is still normal, and monitoring rather than treating.

en: PT, INR and PTT: understanding clotting tests
angle: Essential for anyone on warfarin, which is still widely used regionally. INR target ranges by indication in a table, what makes INR swing including food and antibiotics, and red flags for bleeding.

en: Troponin: the test that confirms a heart attack
angle: Emergency context. High sensitivity troponin, serial testing over hours, and the vital message that chest pain means going to hospital rather than waiting for a lab appointment. Strong red-flag callout.

en: Stool analysis: parasites, blood and what the report means
angle: Intestinal parasites remain common regionally. Cover ova and parasite examination, occult blood, and named regional parasites including amoeba and giardia. Practical hygiene and water safety.

en: H. pylori testing: breath, stool, blood or endoscopy
angle: H. pylori prevalence is among the highest in the world in parts of the region. Compare the four test types in a table including which confirms eradication, and why the blood antibody test cannot.

en: Semen analysis: how to read a male fertility report
angle: High search volume, low quality Arabic coverage, and a topic men research privately. WHO reference values in a table, abstinence period, why one abnormal sample means little, and the need to repeat.

en: Type 2 diabetes: a complete guide for the Middle East
angle: Cornerstone page. The region has some of the highest prevalence on earth. Diagnosis thresholds, HbA1c targets, complications, and the realities of managing it where insulin supply and clinic access vary. Cite IDF Atlas regional figures with a bar chart comparing regional countries.

en: Prediabetes: the window where you can still turn it around
angle: Hopeful, action-oriented, huge audience. The exact HbA1c and fasting glucose bands on a range-scale, the evidence that lifestyle change beats medication at this stage, and a realistic regional food plan.

en: Diabetic foot: preventing the complication that costs limbs
angle: Amputation rates are high regionally. Daily inspection routine as a steps visual, what a neuropathic ulcer looks like, footwear in hot climates, and an urgent red-flag callout.

en: Diabetes and your eyes: catching retinopathy before it blinds
angle: Screening intervals as a timeline, the fact that vision loss appears only late, and the availability of screening regionally.

en: Fatty liver: the silent condition behind rising liver disease
angle: Very high and rising regional prevalence tied to obesity and sugary drinks. Grades of fatty liver, the reversibility message, and the link to diabetes. Bar chart of regional prevalence with sources.

en: Chronic kidney disease: the five stages explained
angle: Diabetes and hypertension are the main causes and both are epidemic regionally. Stage table by eGFR, dialysis access realities, and the painkiller and herbal remedy risk.

en: Gout: stopping the attacks and preventing the next one
angle: Acute attack versus long-term urate lowering, the common mistake of stopping allopurinol during an attack, and regional diet including organ meats and sugary drinks.

angle: Vitamin D deficiency and low activity make this regionally significant, especially in women. T-score range-scale, calcium and vitamin D, fall prevention.

en: Acid reflux and GERD: causes, treatment and when to worry
angle: Very high search volume. Lifestyle triggers including late heavy meals which is a regional eating pattern, PPI use and overuse, and alarm symptoms warranting endoscopy.

en: Underactive thyroid: symptoms, treatment and monitoring
angle: Pairs with the TSH guide. Levothyroxine timing and absorption, why iron and calcium interfere, and re-testing intervals as a timeline.

en: Overactive thyroid: Graves disease and the treatment choices
angle: Antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, surgery compared in a table. Thyroid storm as a red-flag callout.

en: Heart failure: what it means and how to live with it
angle: Ejection fraction explained, daily weight monitoring as the practical self-management tool, salt and fluid, and worsening red flags.

en: Brucellosis (Malta fever): the raw milk infection
angle: Classic regional disease, strongly tied to unpasteurised milk and fresh cheese. Undulant fever pattern on a timeline, the long antibiotic course and why people stop too early, and prevention around home dairy.

angle: Significant regional carrier rates. Decode the confusing serology panel in a table (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc, HBeAg), vaccination, and family screening.

en: Tuberculosis: symptoms, testing and the full course
angle: Latent versus active TB, the six-month regimen and why stopping early creates resistance, and the crowding and displacement drivers regionally.

en: Typhoid fever: water, food and the fever that climbs

en: Bilharzia (schistosomiasis): the freshwater parasite

en: Cholera: recognising it and preventing death from dehydration

en: Urinary tract infection: symptoms, testing and treatment
angle: Very high volume, especially among women. Distinguish simple cystitis from pyelonephritis, when a urine culture is needed, and the resistance problem from repeated self-medication.

en: Food poisoning: what to do and when it is serious
angle: Heat and unreliable cold chains make this regionally frequent, and it spikes at large gatherings and weddings. Timeline by organism, rehydration, and red flags.

en: Malaria: symptoms, testing and prevention
angle: Endemic in Sudan and Yemen, and a travel risk elsewhere. Rapid diagnostic tests, the danger of falciparum, and prevention with nets and repellents.

en: Dengue fever: the mosquito illness spreading in the Gulf
angle: Rising in Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Sudan. Warning signs of severe dengue as a red-flag callout, the specific danger of taking ibuprofen or aspirin, and mosquito control around the home.

en: Leishmaniasis: preventing the sandfly bite

en: Scabies: the itch that spreads through a household

en: Sickle cell disease: crises, care and carrier status

en: G6PD deficiency (favism): the foods and drugs to avoid

angle: Stunting rates are high in Yemen, Sudan and among displaced populations. How to read percentiles, what crossing centiles means, and the critical first 1000 days.

angle: Resurgent regionally despite abundant sun, driven by covering, indoor life and prolonged breastfeeding without supplementation. Signs, supplementation doses by age, and prevention.

angle: Freely sold and freely overused. Kidney, stomach and blood pressure risks, the dengue and chickenpox cautions, and safer alternatives.

angle: Pairs with the resistance article but from the patient decision angle. A table of common illnesses against whether antibiotics help, and how to finish or not finish a course per current guidance.

angle: First-line diabetes drug everywhere. Taking it with food, the gradual dose increase that avoids most side effects, B12 depletion over years, and Ramadan adjustment.

angle: Adherence is poor because of fear. Absolute versus relative risk explained honestly, real versus attributed muscle symptoms, and monitoring.

angle: Absorption is the whole game: empty stomach, gap from coffee, iron, calcium. Steps visual. Re-testing at six weeks on a timeline.

angle: Table of onset, peak and duration by type. Injection site rotation as a steps visual. Hypoglycaemia red-flag callout. Cold storage in hot climates and during power cuts, which is a real regional problem.

angle: Most people use inhalers wrong, which makes the medicine worthless. Pure steps visuals for MDI, spacer and dry powder devices.

angle: Genuinely regional and almost unwritten. What heat does to insulin, antibiotics and inhalers, car glove boxes, power cuts, and travel with a cool bag. Table of storage requirements.

angle: A serious regional problem, worse where supply chains have broken down. Packaging checks as a steps visual, buying from licensed pharmacies, and reporting. Cite WHO substandard and falsified medicines work.

angle: Practical companion to the anaemia articles. Table of regional foods by iron content, haem versus non-haem absorption, and the tea-with-meals problem which is a major regional habit that blocks iron.

angle: Deficiency is common where diets are cereal-heavy. Signs, food sources, and the role in child diarrhoea.

angle: Culturally central and heavily searched. Honest nutrition including sugar content and glycaemic impact for diabetics, fibre and potassium benefits, and the Ramadan role. Correct the exaggerated claims.

en: Olive oil: what the evidence actually supports

angle: Regionally specific and practical. Dehydration signs, urine colour as a range-scale, the outdoor worker risk, and why sugary drinks fail as replacement.

angle: Cuts through a huge and profitable noise. Table of common supplements against actual evidence, who genuinely needs which, and the harm from excess vitamin A and D megadoses.

en: Postpartum depression: more than baby blues
angle: Under-recognised and stigmatised regionally. Distinguish baby blues from depression on a timeline, screening, and the message that it is treatable and not a failure of motherhood.

en: Breastfeeding: getting it working and common problems
angle: Attachment, supply worries which drive most early formula use, mastitis, and feeding while fasting in Ramadan which is a genuinely regional question.

en: Child malnutrition: recognising it and refeeding safely
angle: Acute in Yemen, Sudan and Gaza. MUAC measurement, distinguishing wasting from stunting, refeeding syndrome danger, and therapeutic feeding programmes.

en: Newborn jaundice: normal, and when it is dangerous
angle: Very common and occasionally catastrophic, and G6PD deficiency raises the regional stakes. Timeline of normal versus pathological onset, phototherapy, and an urgent red-flag callout.

en: Blood thinners: warfarin, the newer drugs and staying safe
angle: Warfarin versus DOACs in a table, INR monitoring, food and drug interactions, bleeding red flags, and what to do before dental or surgical procedures.

en: Painkillers and your kidneys: the damage nobody warns about
angle: Chronic NSAID use is a major and preventable cause of regional kidney disease, driven by free over-the-counter availability. Which painkillers, how much, who is most at risk, and safer options.

en: Flu (influenza): symptoms, treatment and when the vaccine matters
angle: Seasonal timing: October to March across the region, so this is the page people search now. Separate flu from a common cold with a comparison table (onset, fever, aches, fatigue). Be blunt that antibiotics do nothing for flu, a widespread regional habit. Who is high risk (pregnancy, over 65, diabetes, asthma, young children) and why the annual vaccine is worth it for them. Red-flag callout for breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion, dehydration in children. Timeline of a typical flu week.

en: Tonsillitis and strep throat: viral or bacterial, and when you need antibiotics
angle: Most sore throats are viral, yet antibiotics are bought over the counter for nearly all of them. Explain the Centor or FeverPAIN style signs that point to strep, the rapid strep test, and why a full course matters when strep is confirmed: rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease are still seen in parts of the region, cite regional rheumatic heart disease evidence. Red-flag callout: drooling, can not swallow, muffled voice, one-sided swelling (quinsy). When tonsillectomy is considered.

en: Sinusitis: symptoms, how long it lasts and when antibiotics help
angle: Acute sinusitis is usually viral and clears in 2 to 3 weeks. Explain the 10 day rule and the 'double worsening' pattern that suggests bacterial infection. Dust storms and allergic rhinitis drive chronic sinus symptoms in the region. Steps for saline rinsing done safely (boiled or bottled water, a real regional concern). Red flags: swelling around the eye, severe headache with stiff neck, double vision. Distinguish from dental pain and migraine.

en: Ear infection in children: signs, pain relief and when to see a doctor
angle: Acute otitis media is the commonest reason children get antibiotics. Signs in a baby who can not talk (pulling ear, crying at night, fever). Watchful waiting for 48 to 72 hours is standard in many guidelines for mild cases over age 2, explain when antibiotics are needed instead. Never put oil, garlic or anything else in the ear, a common home remedy. Red flags: swelling behind the ear, stiff neck, discharge with high fever. Glue ear and hearing after repeated infections.

en: Head lice in children: how to get rid of them and stop them coming back
angle: Back-to-school season. Lice are not a sign of poor hygiene, say so plainly because shame stops parents acting. Wet combing method as steps, how approved treatments are used in general terms, why kerosene, petrol and insecticides meant for animals or crops are dangerous (real regional practice, cite poisoning evidence if found). Checking the whole family, what does and does not need washing. Table of myths vs facts.

en: Heart attack warning signs: what to do in the first minutes
angle: Highest-stakes page on the site. Classic and atypical symptoms (women, people with diabetes may have no chest pain). Steps for the first minutes: call the emergency number, chew aspirin only if advised by emergency services and not allergic, do not drive yourself. Why time to hospital matters (door to balloon). Regional evidence: heart attacks occur at younger ages in the Middle East than in the West, cite Gulf RACE or similar. Link to troponin test and emergency numbers articles. Red-flag callout up top.

en: Kidney stones: symptoms, treatment and how to stop them coming back
angle: The Gulf and Middle East sit in the global 'stone belt' because of heat and dehydration, cite regional prevalence. Renal colic pain pattern, blood in urine, when stones pass alone by size (table of size vs chance of passing). Prevention: fluid targets in heat, salt, oxalate foods common in the regional diet, citrate. Red flags: fever with stone pain (infected obstructed kidney is an emergency), no urine. Types of stones and what the stone analysis tells you.

en: Constipation: causes, quick relief and when to worry
angle: Digestive health is the biggest gap on the site. Define constipation properly (Bristol stool chart as a table). Common causes in the region: low fibre diets heavy in white bread and rice, low water intake in heat, painkillers containing codeine, iron tablets. Steps that work: fibre, fluid, movement, toilet posture. Warn against long-term senna or herbal laxative teas (link to senna article). Red flags for bowel cancer: blood, weight loss, change in habit after 50, anaemia. Constipation in children and in pregnancy as short sections.

en: Haemorrhoids (piles): symptoms, home treatment and when you need a doctor
angle: Very high search volume in Arabic and a topic people are too embarrassed to ask about. Internal vs external, what bleeding looks like. Home care steps (fibre, sitz baths, not straining, not sitting on the toilet with a phone). Over-the-counter creams in general terms, avoid long-term steroid creams. Why rectal bleeding must never be assumed to be piles after 40 or 50 (bowel cancer). Treatment options: banding, surgery, table comparing them. Pregnancy and piles.

en: Stomach ulcer: symptoms, causes and how it is treated
angle: Peptic ulcer disease. The two main causes are H. pylori (very common in the region, cite regional prevalence) and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen and diclofenac bought without prescription. Link to h-pylori-test-explained and ibuprofen-nsaids-risks, do not repeat them. Symptoms vs reflux. How eradication therapy works in general terms and why the full course plus a test of cure matters. Red flags: vomiting blood or coffee grounds, black tarry stools, sudden severe abdominal pain.

en: Coeliac disease: symptoms, the blood test and living gluten-free
angle: Coeliac disease is under-diagnosed in the Middle East, where wheat bread is a staple. Cite regional prevalence studies. Symptoms beyond the gut: iron deficiency anaemia that does not respond to iron, short stature in children, osteoporosis. The tTG-IgA blood test and why you must keep eating gluten until tested. Range-scale is not needed; use a table of hidden gluten in regional foods (freekeh, bulgur, burghul, couscous, some spice mixes). Gluten-free Arab staples that are safe.

en: Pregnancy blood test (beta hCG): what your number means
angle: Massive Arabic query (تحليل الحمل الرقمي). When to test after a missed period, home urine test vs blood test, what quantitative beta hCG levels mean by week (table with wide ranges, cite source), why one number means little and the doubling pattern over 48 hours matters. Low or slowly rising hCG, ectopic pregnancy red flags (one-sided pain, shoulder tip pain, fainting) in a bad callout. Range-scale for the pregnant vs not pregnant cut-off (under 5 mIU/mL negative, over 25 positive).

en: AMH test: what it says about your egg reserve, and what it does not
angle: Very high Arabic search interest (تحليل مخزون البيض). Explain AMH honestly: it estimates egg quantity, not quality, and it does not predict natural fertility well in women not trying IVF. Age-based reference table with source. Low AMH is not infertility. High AMH and PCOS link (link pcos-guide). Units differ between labs (ng/mL vs pmol/L), conversion. When the test is genuinely useful: before IVF, before cancer treatment, family planning conversations. Range-scale.

en: Prolactin test: causes of high prolactin and what happens next
angle: Common Arabic query (هرمون الحليب). How to prepare (stress, sleep, nipple stimulation, exercise raise it, so morning rested sample), why a mildly high result is often repeated. Causes table: pregnancy, breastfeeding, medicines (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, some antidepressants), hypothyroidism, pituitary prolactinoma, macroprolactin. Symptoms in women and in men. Range-scale with units and a note that ranges vary by lab. When an MRI is ordered.

en: Hair loss: which blood tests to ask for and what they mean
angle: Huge Arabic query (تحاليل تساقط الشعر). Ferritin, vitamin D, TSH, CBC, zinc, and in women testosterone and other androgens when PCOS is suspected. Explain which have strong evidence and which are mostly upsold by labs and clinics (honest about biotin and vitamin panels). Table: test, what it looks for, when it is worth doing. Telogen effluvium after fever, childbirth or crash dieting, and the 3 month delay. Pattern hair loss in men and women. Red flags: patches with scaling, scarring, sudden loss of eyebrows.

en: PSA test: what a high result means for your prostate
angle: Men's health is a gap on the site. Explain PSA plainly, what raises it other than cancer (enlarged prostate, infection, recent ejaculation, cycling, catheter), age-related ranges as a table with source, free vs total PSA. The honest debate about screening: shared decision from about 50, earlier with family history. What happens after a raised result (repeat, MRI, biopsy) as a timeline. Symptoms of an enlarged prostate. Range-scale.
